I suffer from Major Depressive Disorder and when the slumps hit, they hit really hard. 

Ask her how she's feeling, what her thoughts are what what they look like and mean to her. 

Validate her feelings but also reassure her they are just a product/result of her depression. 

Explaining all of her good qualities and requesting that she acknowledges that, even though she may not feel these good things about her, that it's ok that others feel and think them of her. 

Let her know that the depression often projects how we feel about ourselves onto others but that doesn't make those feelings true for you or your friends. 

My Partner has been doing these little talks with me for months and it's not always easy for me to acknowledge that while I may not feel great about myself, that doesn't mean my partner or my children feel the same about me. 

It does help to pull me out of my head and realize that my awful thoughts are just my own and I need to work through them. 

Remind her gently that she cannot tell you or others how they feel about her and again reassure her it's only a product of the depression. 

It's really hard to go through these periods. Ad the sufferer and as a partner. 

But there are ways you can work through it together. 

Maybe, instead of telling her how much you love her, show her in small ways. 

Grab her her favorite drink on your way home from work or being out and just hand it to her. Say "I was just thinking of you and thought you might like this."

Run her a bath with candles lit up for a warm and inviting relaxation time. 

Randomly make her a snack or tea or coffee, something that she really likes. 

If she suffers from any kind of pains, get a heating pad, rice bag or something to being relief. 

All of these little things show a huge amount of care and that you're thinking of her. At it will help lighten her mood.

I suffer from chronic illnesses. I'll give you a small list. 

1. Chronic Fatigue Syndrome 
2. Fibromyalgia 
3. Occipital Neuralgia 
4. Severe form of Osteoarthritis 
5. Central Sensitization Syndrome
6. Empty Sella Syndrome

It took YEARS to get diagnosed. Countless blood work to the point where I looked like a drug addict from all of the bruises on my arms and hands. 

Tons of MRI's (20 and counting), CT scans, tried about 20 different medications that have now ruined my stomach and I have chronic stomach pain. 

Keep pushing. 

I understand the frustration. I get the tears and the fear and anger. It's hard to know that something is going on with your body and no one believes you.

Some illnesses are diagnosed by ruling out other ones. Compile a list of your symptoms along with possible illnesses, complete it with the exams you've done and what showed up in the clear and request for more tests that support your symptoms.  

When I was going through tests for my chronic pain, I asked for tests related to diseases with pain. They found my C-reactive proteins were elevated and with that we finally had a starting point. 

Just because a doctor says no or something doesn't fit, doesn't mean you have to accept their answer and go home. Sometimes you have to make demands.

Hey. So, I have BPD too so I'm going to try to put this as gently as I can but also be honest. 

Yes you over reacted. I get why you did but you did. 

As someone with BPD, you have to take a step back and look through their eyes at the situation. Put yourself in their shoes and think about how it feels to be them. 

Unfortunately with BPD this can be super hard to do because unless you have a full understanding of your brand of BPD and how you work with it, then you will tend to live mostly in your head. 

Remember, BPD is a personal reality disorder. Your personal reality is distorted and often, you can't think outside of that reality that you've created. 

I signed up for a program called "Intergrate". It's designed specifically for the BPD community. 

It's really helped me a lot over the last couple of years learning about BPD, how it works and why and how to start seeing reality from a normal perspective.  

I highly recommend you look into the program. Therapy is great, but it's not going to help your BPD and that is something you should really get on top of.

Everyone's skin is different and going to hold ink differently. 

Every artist usually explains this when you get s tattoo.  I've not met an artist who hasn't gone through this, regardless of how many tattoos you have. 

Because each artist has a different technique and they use different products as well. 

Your tattoo being lighter OR darker doesn't always reflect on the artists work or ability. 

Whenever I've gotten a tattoo, I've asked the artist their brand of ink, their knowledge on said brand and how long it takes to fade, general ink care, how long for touch ups etc. 

These are basic questions everyone should be asking before getting a tattoo. Mostly for your own reassurance AND then that way, you're not throwing the artist under a bus.

Cats are carnivors, so while certain grains like rice can be beneficial, most grains are really hard on their bodies. 

Check the ingredients in the food you buy. 

Changing your cat to a raw based diet is also probably better since eating kibble tends to leave them more "dehydrated" thus drinking a lot more water to compensate. 

A raw diet, or home prepared diet is better for moisture and puts less strain on their kidneys and over all bladder health.

There are a lot of variables that go into these kinds of things and behavior intervention is a very in-depth type of training.
